summary: The imperative is built from the “you” form of the present: drop the prefix تَـ (تَذْهَبُ → ذْهَبْ) and, if the word now starts with two consonants, put a helping alif in front — اِ when the present vowel is a or i (اِذْهَبْ, اِنْتَظِرْ, اِمْشِ), اُ when it is u (اُدْخُلْ, اُخْرُجْ, اُرْكُضْ). The ending says who is spoken to: nothing (sukūn) to a man, -ī to a woman, -ū to several men or a mixed group, -na to several women: اِذْهَبْ / اِذْهَبِي / اِذْهَبُوا / اِذْهَبْنَ. Verbs whose present has a vowel after the prefix need no helping alif: form III سَافِرْ, غَادِرْ (from تُسَافِرُ, تُغَادِرُ), hollow قُدْ, عُدْ (with a short vowel before a consonant ending, long before a vowel: قُودِي, عُودُوا). A weak last letter falls away to a man: اِمْشِ, اِبْقَ, اِشْتَرِ. Two common irregulars: كُلْ (eat!) from أَكَلَ, and “come!” is تَعَالَ (تَعَالَيْ, تَعَالَوْا), not the rare جِئْ. The helping alif is hamzat al-waṣl: it is said at the start, silent after a vowel. Arabic has no polite form like German Sie: politeness comes from words — مِنْ فَضْلِكَ / مِنْ فَضْلِكِ, لَوْ سَمَحْتَ. “Don’t …!” is لَا + the jussive (لَا تَذْهَبْ), a form of a later lesson.

blocks.title: Please.
blocks.text: Add مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (to a man), مِنْ فَضْلِكِ (to a woman), مِنْ فَضْلِكُمْ (to several) or لَوْ سَمَحْتَ: اِنْتَظِرْ قَلِيلًا، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. To invite someone in, تَفَضَّلْ is the polite word.

blocks.title: The helping alif is silent after a vowel.
blocks.text: At the start of a sentence it is said: اِذْهَبْ (iḏhab). After a vowel it disappears in speech and loses its vowel sign in writing: وَاذْهَبْ (wa-ḏhab). Form III and hollow verbs have no such alif: سَافِرْ, قُدْ.

blocks.title: No pronoun, four forms.
blocks.text: The ending already says who is meant, so there is no “you”: اِجْلِسْ / اِجْلِسِي — German setz dich / setzen Sie sich has a polite form; Arabic has gender and number instead.
The plural -ū is written with a silent alif, as in the past: اِذْهَبُوا, اُدْخُلُوا, قُودُوا; the women form ends in -na: اِذْهَبْنَ, قُدْنَ.

askYourself: Who am I talking to: a man, a woman, several men or a mixed group, several women?
What is the present “you” form? تَذْهَبُ, تَدْخُلُ, تُسَافِرُ, تَقُودُ, تَمْشِي …
Drop تَـ / تُـ. Two consonants at the start now? → add اِ (present vowel a or i) or اُ (present vowel u).
Hollow verb? Short vowel when the ending is sukūn or -na (قُدْ, قُدْنَ), long before -ī / -ū (قُودِي, قُودُوا).
Weak last letter? It falls away to a man: اِمْشِ, اِبْقَ, اِشْتَرِ.
Polite? Add مِنْ فَضْلِكَ / مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.

traps: *اِدْخُلْ → اُدْخُلْ: the present vowel u gives the helping vowel u.
*اِسَافِرْ → سَافِرْ: form III needs no helping alif.
*قُودْ → قُدْ: a hollow verb shortens its vowel before sukūn.
اِمْشِي is to a woman; to a man it is اِمْشِ.
“Don’t go!” is not *لَا اِذْهَبْ but لَا تَذْهَبْ (the jussive, a later lesson).

quiz.why: To one woman the command ends in -ī.
The present is تَدْخُلُ (u), so the helping vowel is u.
Hollow verb: short u before the sukūn.
The weak last letter falls away to a man; اِبْقَيْ is to a woman.
أَكَلَ has the short irregular command كُلْ.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew builds the command from the future stem too: לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ (go!) — in speech the future often serves as a command (תֵּלֵךְ). Like Arabic it has masculine and feminine forms.
German: geh! / geht! / gehen Sie! — a polite Sie-form but no gender. Arabic: four forms by gender and number, politeness by words (مِنْ فَضْلِكَ).
Chinese has no command form: the bare verb (走！), 请 for “please”, 吧 to soften, 别 / 不要 for “don’t”.
The command comes from the present “you” form (lesson 7).
مِنْ فَضْلِكَ / مِنْ فَضْلِكِ and لَوْ سَمَحْتَ change with the listener (lesson 2).
